Remember when I said that I was done signing up for every new service that comes along? Yeah, me too. But...
Today I learned about quxnet via the always interesting Linkdump, from 82MHz, who linked to Quxnet Is a Breath of Fresh Air | moddedbear.com. Of course I created an account immediately  because how could I not? I mean, there's an SSH/TUI interface for it. Sold!

Quxnet has everything. Boards, mail, photo galleries, links, blogs, an RSS reader, and more. It looks super-retro cool, which adds to the vibe. I don't know what I want out of it yet, but if it can remain "A private network with old internet manners." then I can see it becoming a fun new place to hang out.
There are still fewer than 1,000 people there, so naturally things are cordial and sufficiently nerdy and polite. I hope it stays polite, but I worry that with popularity comes conflicting views from people who "We" don't agree with, and once the finger-pointing starts, things tend to go south. I hope it doesn't happen that way.
But for now it's clever, fun, nerdy, and new, so I'm in. https://quxnet.net/u/jbaty.

articles.description:
new Emacs trick from Emacs Dwelling. Well, new to me. It turns out it’s been in Emacs since 28.1 so for about four and a half years.


Here’s the problem. When you call isearch it starts searching at the current point location to the bottom of the file. You can cause it to wrap around and continue searching at the top of the file but this isn’t always convenient. As a result, many people always start their search by moving to the top of the buffer first. But this isn’t always convenient either. For example, if you quit the search you go back to the top of the file, not where you started.


Sometimes you want a bit more control: perhaps you want to start at the first match or the last match and if you quit, you’d like to be back where you started. Well this is Emacs so of course you can do that. The nice thing is that it’s already built in. There are no packages to install, you just enable it my setting isearch-allow-motion to t.


You can start the search at any of:


The current point position
The first match in the file
The last match in the file
The first match before the window
The first match after the window
articles.title: Irreal: Controlling Where Isearch Starts Searching

taking some data that she’s collected and analysing it to extract useful information. For some reason I really like that sort of thing and am always doing it myself with my own data.


In Chua’s case, she wanted to know how many Emacs News entries she’s written and plot them over time. It’s a little more difficult than you might think. First of all, she didn’t have the complete Emacs News index so she had to recreate the missing parts by converting the HTML entries into Org mode. She did that with a standard Unix pipeline using Pandoc.


Once she had everything in Org mode, she wrote some Elisp to extract the needed information and put it in a table. From there, it was easy to produce a graph showing how may entries she wrote by year. You can even see the years her daughter was a toddler because the number of entries went down for a couple of years. As Chua says, “Babies sleep a lot; toddlers, not so much.”


Take a look at Chua’s post to see all the code and the final graph. The data is mostly useful only for Chua just as mine is useful mostly for me but the way she goes about analyzing the data is useful to anyone that needs to take some data and massage it.
articles.title: Irreal: Analyzing Emacs News

articles.description:
building and using Org capture templates. What’s interesting about his approach is that his template prompts for certain information—customer ID and site location in his example—captures that information in some local variables, and uses those variables to customize the capture for the particular customer.


His two main tools for doing this are:


The %^{PROMPT|A|B|...} placeholder to prompt for data.
The %(EXP) placeholder to execute the Elisp expression EXP.
ms/set-var, prompts the user for the value of a variable, creates the variable, sets its value, and returns the value. This is different from the %^{...} placeholder in that it captures the value of the user’s answer for later use. The other helper functions make use of the captured variables.


Take a look at Schell’s post to see the functions and how the whole thing hangs together. His needs may be more complicated than normal but the ideas he uses to solve them are handy and applicable to many—even simpler—situations.


I’ve used all the placeholders that uses in my own templates but the idea of capturing a variable for later reuse in the template is new to me. It’s a neat idea and definitely worth knowing.
articles.title: Irreal: Variables In Org Capture

If you want maximalist themes in terms of colour, check my ef-themes
package. For something in-between, which I consider the best “default

Package name (GNU ELPA): doric-themes
Sample pictures: https://protesilaos.com/emacs/doric-themes-pictures
Git repository: https://github.com/protesilaos/doric-themes
Backronym: Doric Only Really Intensifies Conservatively … themes.
Below are the release notes.
Update to doric-themes version 1.4.0
The new doric-meadow and doric-mountain themes
doric-meadow is a light theme with yellow and green colours, while
doric-mountain has a similar albeit dark palette. They expand the
collection of the Doric themes to cover even more styles and
preferences.
Diff colours are refined
I improved the inter-theme consistency of all colours that apply to
diffs, such as those shown in diff-mode, ediff, and magit buffers.
Before, some themes were needlessly more subtle than others while
certain colours could be hard to discern in some situations. For
example, if the diff-hl package was in use and the fringe was set to
a thin line.
Other packages also benefit from this review, such as my pulsar and
lin.
Matching parentheses are distinct from the active region
The highlight of matching parentheses produced by show-paren-mode is
now distinct from the active region. The same is true for the current
line, per hl-line-mode.
The doric-themes-define-theme should not fail in certain cases
I fixed an issue that was reported to me by Amin Bandali where the
doric-themes-define-theme was failing to instantiate a theme in the
macroexpanded code.
The bg-accent and fg-accent palette entries are renamed
This is relevant for those who rely on doric-themes-with-colors. The
new names are bg-accent-primary and fg-accent-primary. The old
ones will not longer work.

articles.description:
dictating into Emacs. She starts by quoting Matt Weber on how he writes better than he speaks. Chua can relate and so can I. We both feel the same way. As I’ve said before, “…my written thoughts are always much better organized than my spoken ones…”.


Being who she is, Chua resolved to fix this by arranging to dictate her posts into Emacs. As you can imagine, she encountered all sorts of problems along the way but was mainly able to find solutions for them. You can check her post—and Weber’s—to see how they’re doing that.


When I read Chua’s post, I thought, “maybe I should do that too” but then I realized that I don’t want to dictate my text. The truth is, I enjoy writing a lot more than I do speaking and I especially enjoy writing with Emacs. Although it’s not always obvious, I do a lot of revising on my posts as I write them and I usually try to make a final editing pass at least one day after I’ve written them. Speaking, on the other hands, feels more like “one and done” to me. I know that I could dictate a post and then edit the result but it’s not the same. And in any event, as I say, I enjoy writing a lot more than I enjoy talking.


I suppose, as Chua says, the day may come when ever encroaching old age, disease, or accident may make typing hard or impossible and I may be forced to consider dictation but until then, I’m happy to continue typing my text.

I've just made a very small update to
blogmore.el to fix a small bug,
and also to update some deprecated code.
The blogmore-new command inserts the result of expanding a template into
the buffer when making a new post, and I've not touched that template since
I started writing blogmore.el. This includes not updating it when I
switched much of the frontmatter-handling code over to proper YAML parsing.
The problem here was that the title didn't get quotes around it, which
became an issue if there was something like a : in the title; any
subsequent attempt to modify frontmatter properties would throw an error.
So this release ensures that the title and the date get quoted right away. I
guess, at some point, I should rework this code so that it uses the
frontmatter-handling code to set up those properties and, instead, just uses
the template for the main body.
I've also changed all uses of things like when-let and if-let to use
when-let* and if-let*. It seems that, as of Emacs 31.1, the former are
deprecated.

articles.description:
really hate being spied on by web sites and other on-line entities. I’m pretty sure this misbehavior won’t be legal much longer but I’m equally sure that the on-line advertising industry won’t go gentle into that good night and will find ways to nibble around the edges of whatever laws get passed.


Happily, there’s Magic Lasso which pretty much solves the problem for Safari users. That would be the end of the story except that I use XWidgets with mu4e to read HTML emails and Elfeed entries through the wonderful elfeed-webkit. They work nicely but now Magic Lasso is no longer filtering their content so cookies and trackers are being accumulated. For the longest time I couldn’t find where they were being stored. I finally stumbled on its location and discovered that it was a simple text file that could simply be deleted.


The problem was that I had to remember to do it and more specifically, where the file was located. I finally stopped being stupid and wrote a simple function to delete the file:


(defun jcs-kill-cookies ()
  "Delete the cookies from Webkit"
  (interactive)
  (delete-file ".emacs.d/url/cookies")
  (message "Cookies deleted."))

jcs-kill-cookies when I quit elfeed so I don’t have to remember to do it manually. All of this is trivial, of course, but it’s another example of sanding down your workflow to make it as simple as possible. Now things pretty much take care of themselves. I suppose I should figure out a way to delete cookies after email too but for now I’m happy that the problem is mostly solved.

articles.description:
about debugging your init file. The main problem, he says, is that he sometimes makes a change that results in unbalanced parentheses. Often he doesn’t discover this until the next time he reboots Emacs, something he doesn’t do often.


He says that his usual method for finding the problem was to do what amounts to a binary search on his init file: He comments out half the init file. If the problem occurs, he repeats the process with the commented potion; otherwise he continues with the uncommented half. But then he discovered the built-in function check-parens that checks for unbalanced delimiters in the current buffer. That’s a nifty solution to Ridenour’s problem that I didn’t know about. Another tool in the toolbox.


The other thing about his post is that it reminded me of a package I wrote about in 2015 from Artur Malabarba: elisp-bug-hunter. I haven’t used it in a while but every time I do, it works perfectly and invariably finds the error often without any further action. What it does is automate the binary search that Ridenour used to hunt down his unbalanced parentheses but it works for any problem.


If the problem throws an error, elisp-bug-hunter will find it without any user input but for more complicated situations, you can specify a predicate to indicate whether the current run succeeded or not. I load it early in my init so it will be available if there is a problem.


So the take away from this post is two really useful debugging tools: check-parens for finding unbalanced delimiters and elisp-debug-hunter. Everyone should know these tools.
articles.title: Irreal: Debugging Init.el Files

articles.description:
There’s a Terry Pratchett quote I love, about how all contemporary fantasy is written under the influence of The Lord of the Rings. “Tolkien has become a sort of mountain, appearing in all subsequent fantasy in the way that Mt. Fuji appears so often in Japanese prints,” Pratchett wrote. “Sometimes it’s big and up close. Sometimes it’s a shape on the horizon. Sometimes it’s not there at all, which means that the artist either has made a deliberate decision against the mountain, which is interesting in itself, or is in fact standing on Mt. Fuji.”
I think this holds true for all genre fiction; there are giants of the genre, who introduced basically all of the tropes, fully formed, and anyone working in that genre is constantly in conversation with those tropes. Every ghost story is in communion with Henry James; every haunted house owes a debt to Shirley Jackson. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing. Cliches become cliches for a reason, and it can be rewarding as a reader to spot the influences.
We are primed to expect the expected, just by picking up a ghost story in the first place. “Ghost stories might not all use the same words,” Malerman has one of his characters observe, “but they all sound like the same words because it’s the ghost we think about, not the words.”

articles.description:
What was your favorite video review controversy at this past summer's World Cup? Was it when Egypt had the best goal in their history disallowed for a foul committed by an unrelated guy 15 seconds before the big moment, when Iran lost to that same Egypt side over a totally fake offsides call, when the mouth-covering red card rule was applied against a Paraguayan player but not against an England player, or when Donald Trump personally lobbied FIFA to get a red card against Folarin Balogun rescinded? It's hard to choose from such a bounty of options. 
The 2026 World Cup represented a nadir in the evolution of soccer as theatrical product, with interminable replay reviews bringing the action to a halt in the name of adjudicating decisions that a referee couldn't possibly make. The world has been told that the death of theater is the price of fairness.
I hate this stuff, especially because VAR is wrong all the time. The counterargument would be that without VAR, referees would miss even more stuff and that the world would see big, consequential calls get blown without the ability to review them. On this week's episode of Only If You Get Caught, we examine the most famous missed call in the history of soccer as a way of making the argument against VAR. Our show is often accused of being pro-cheating, which is usually mistaking curiosity for endorsement. But in this case the charges are correct: We absolutely love the Hand of God.
articles.title: How The Best Moment Of Cheating In Soccer History Makes The Case Against VAR

That is a lot of money. His latest ex-wife, Princess Santiago, with whom Pierce engaged in a public and nasty paternity dispute, is reportedly asking a court to award her another $40,000 in legal fees, and for $10,000 to hire a forensic accountant. articles.description:
It's bad enough that Pat McAfee is so omnipresent and obnoxious, but does he also have to be so thin-skinned?
ESPN's prize hog used Monday's episode of his daily talk show to complain about what a bad experience he had at the University of Utah when he was there for College GameDay this past weekend. More specifically, McAfee was aggravated because the school had posted a video (now deleted) in which a couple of students were prompted to do an impression of him. "He's gonna say a corny line," said one student who was predicting McAfee's GameDay pick. "He's gonna be like, 'Houston, we got a problem. Gimme the Utah Utes.'" For the record, McAfee picked the visiting Cougars in Saturday's game, but Utah won, 21-13.
Another student mocked McAfee for his well-worn bit of taking off his shirt on set. "Bro, Pat, we love you, bro, but keep the shirt on. No one's trying to see that. We don't care. These are college kids, bro. Keep your shirt on, homie." I have to admit: These youthful Utes had him dead to rights.
articles.title: Pat McAfee Receives Mild Criticism From College Student, Compares It To Charlie Kirk Getting Shot

articles.description: On a hot summer day in August 1972, actor-turned-documentarian William Greaves orchestrated a cocktail party at Duke Ellington’s home. He invited the surviving architects of the Harlem Renaissance and encouraged them to bask in impassioned discussion of the history and legacy of that period. Greaves, along with his son David and two other cameramen, captured 60,000 feet of film of the entire event. Throughout the remainder of his life and career, he wrestled with how to use the footage. At one point he hoped to use it in the award-winning documentary From These Roots (1974), but instead decided to set it aside, giving it room to breathe. Greaves died in 2014 at the age of 87, with the raw footage still unfinished and fragmentary. His son, David, and granddaughter, Liani, then took up the m…
articles.title: The Harlem Renaissance Is Still Alive In ‘Once Upon A Time In Harlem’

articles.description:
In the top of the fifth inning of Monday's Game 3 of the World Series, Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich hustled into second base off a ground ball hit by William Contreras. He was called out on the field, ending the half-inning. The play looked well worth a challenge, but with two outs, I still decided that it would be a good time to take a shower. When I came out of the shower, the Brewers had scored eight two-out runs, extending their lead to 10-0. It went like this: single, single, double, double, single, double, flyout. And then the Rays just had to play through the rest of the game to get to the next one, where they will be fending off a sweep.

https://youtu.be/y_06drhyWDI


The first two games of the series showcased the Brewers' historic skillset as pesky fighters who never go away. Neither of their starters, Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson, were at their best; Game 1 featured some uncharacteristic wobbles in the fundamentals from both teams, and Henderson gave up four runs in the first inning of Game 2. Each game featured some ninth-inning weirdness, with Game 1 ending after a video review and smoke on the field from some overeager celebratory fireworks, and Game 2 ending on an unreviewable checked-swing call with the top of the Tampa Bay lineup up to bat.
articles.title: The Milwaukee Brewers Win At Everything

Sure, the Heat gave up pretty much every asset it had aside from Bam Adebayo to make the trade work, and there were roster issues galore heading into the season, but still. Giannis! Antetokounmpo! How could this fail? It simply couldn't!
Anyway, Miami lost to the Dallas Mavericks on Monday night and dropped to 0-4 for the season. Worse than that, the team has looked lost and overwhelmed in every single game.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vDxNf1bBs6o
articles.title: The Heat Are Drowning

articles.description:
The story begins with a man fixated on the idea of a German Shepherd, which was first bred for its wolf-like appearance and obedience as a worker. He is less invested in the dog as an animal as he is in the dog as a symbol of loyalty and obedience, always valuable traits under an authoritarian regime. He is also interested in tinkering with the dogs to hone them as weapons of war.
I am speaking, of course, of the American entrepreneur Ben Lamm, one of the founders of the new defense technology company Warhound, which has raised $200 million in funding to create genetically modified dogs for the U.S. military, and law enforcement. The promotional art for Warhound is laughably fascist, featuring several German shepherds garbed like Tier 1 operators. They wear tactical vests and protective sunglasses and helmets. Two of the dogs are totally white for reasons that are unclear but also unsettling.
I've written about Ben Lamm before and the gripes I have with his most famous startup, Colossal Biosciences, which has raised hundreds of millions of dollars in ostensible pursuit of its promise to "de-extinct" the mammoth and other flashy prehistorics despite being dishonest about what "de-extinction" really means. Although I did not predict Colossal's next outlandish project would rise to the bar of "genetically-modified murder dogs," I can't say I'm surprised. In classic Colossal fashion, these war dogs do not exist yet. Also in classic Colossal fashion, the company has promised a short timeline: puppies early next year and dogs in military service in two years.
articles.title: More Like A Colossal Piece Of Shit

Newmark founded Craigslist.org in San Francisco way back in 1996 and became the sort of accidental billionaire that the early dot-com boom cranked out with seeming regularity. Some of those billionaires went on to become evil (Mark Zuckerberg), and some of them ended up merely becoming rich loud guys (Mark Cuban). Newmark, who ceded his CEO duties at Craigslist shortly after its founding, has endeavored to keep a lower profile, and a lower net worth, than any of them.

Wildfire is a natural part of California’s environment, and thanks to humankind’s disastrous warping of the planet’s climate, fires will only grow more widespread and destructive in the years to come.

There’s a good chance you’ve heard of Tadich Grill, given that the restaurant is older than San Francisco itself. It’s existed in one form or another since 1849, when it opened under the name Coffee Stand. That was one year before the city of San Francisco was formally incorporated, and 118 years before the restaurant moved to its current location on California Street in the Financial District. Tadich has been doling out fresh seafood and mesquite-grilled slabs of meat to patrons through a lifespan that has included multiple earthquakes, two world wars, Prohibition and multiple pandemics. It’s not merely the oldest restaurant in San Francisco, but in all of California. An eternal landmark. I only needed to walk through its doors on an early evening this August to understand why.

Actually,…

articles.description:
Virtual signalling is often used as an insult, but it’s good to signal your virtues, actually.
A few months back, I read a story on Bluesky from a hispanic woman who’s immigrant mother got lost in the city. Her phone ran of battery, she didn’t speak much English, and she had no idea how to get home.
She approached a young woman with bright blue hair who was able to use her phone’s translation app to get the mother’s address and help her get home.
articles.title: Signal your virtues

articles.description:
There’s an older deaf gentleman in my town who’s very friendly, and likes to communicate with rudimentary hand gestures, but I have a hard time understand what he’s trying to say.
I’d love to learn American Sign Language (ASL) at some point (shoutout King Ron), but until then, I wanted an app that could convert speech into text.
Every transcription app I found required a pretty expensive subscription… so I decided to build my own using web technologies!
articles.title: The SpeechRecognition API

articles.description:
Last week, I needed to make some pretty major updates to a web component in a design system I use for clients.
I’m a big fan of TDD, but I wasn’t mentally in a place to write my tests first.
I decided the easiest thing to do was document how the new component would work… before actually writing any code to implement the updates.
It was an entirely ADHD-driven decision, but it unlocked something for me!
articles.title: Documentation-Driven Development
